'''Leonard Carlitz''' (December 26, 1907 – September 17, 1999) was an American [[mathematician]].  Carlitz supervised 44 doctorates at [[Duke University]] and published more than 770 papers.

== Chronology ==

* 1907 Born [[Philadelphia|Philadelphia, PA]], USA
* 1927 BA, [[University of Pennsylvania]]
* 1930 PhD, University of Pennsylvania, 1930 under Howard Mitchell, who had studied under [[Oswald Veblen]] at [[Princeton University|Princeton]]
* 1930–31 at [[Caltech]] with [[E. T. Bell]]
* 1931 married Clara Skaler
* 1931–32 at [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]] with [[G. H. Hardy]]
* 1932 Joined the faculty of Duke University where he served for 45 years
* 1938 to 1973 Editorial Board [[Duke Mathematical Journal]] (Managing Editor from 1945.)
* 1939 Birth of son Michael
* 1940 Supervision of his first doctoral student E. F. Canaday, awarded 1940
* 1945 Birth of son Robert
* 1964 First [[James B. Duke Professor]] in Mathematics
* 1971 Birth of granddaughter Natasha
* 1977 Supervised his 44th and last doctoral student, Jo Ann Lutz, awarded 1977
* 1977 Retired
* 1982 Birth of granddaughter Ruth
* 1990 Death of wife Clara, after 59 years of marriage
* 1999 September 17 Died in Pittsburgh, PA

== Mathematical work ==
* The [[Drinfeld module#Examples of Drinfeld modules|Carlitz module]] is generalized by the [[Drinfeld module]]
* [[Bernoulli numbers#Assorted identities|An identity]] regarding [[Bernoulli numbers]]
* Carlitz wrote about [[Bessel polynomials]]
* He introduced [[Al-Salam–Carlitz polynomials]].
* [[Bicentric quadrilateral#Carlitz' identity|Carlitz' identity for bicentric quadrilaterals]]
* He conjectured the [[Carlitz-Wan conjecture]], later proved by [[Daqing Wan]].

== Publications ==

Leonard Carlitz published about 771 technical papers comprising approximately 7,000 pages. The effort to edit his collected works, undertaken originally by Professor [[John Brillhart]], is ongoing.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Brawley | first1=Joel V. | authorlink1=Joel Brawley
| last2=Brillhart | first2=John | authorlink2=John Brillhart
| last3=Gould | first3=Henry W. | authorlink3=Henry W. Gould
| title=Recollections of Leonard Carlitz (including: The publications of Leonard Carlitz)
| journal=[[Acta Arithmetica]]
| volume=152
| date=2012
| issue=4
| pages=361–405
| doi=10.4064/aa152-4-3 | doi-access=free}}</ref>

Carlitz' exceptional productivity is described by David Hayes as follows:<ref>{{Citation | last1=Hayes | first1=David R. | title=Leonard Carlitz (1907–1999) | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200111/comm-carlitz.pdf | mr=1870635 | year=2001 | journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] | issn=0002-9920 | volume=48 | issue=11 | pages=1322–1324}}</ref>

{{Blockquote
|text=During the early 1960s, when I was one of his graduate students, Carlitz had a National Science Foundation grant that paid for a half-time secretary. On more than one day I observed him reading a journal paper raising a question that he found of interest, that evening writing up a paper of his own answering the question, and having it typed and sent off to a journal the following day.}}

About 160 articles by Carlitz are about [[finite field]]s. The textbook by Rudolf Lidl and [[Harald Niederreiter]] on the topic<ref>{{citation
| last1=Lidl | first1=Rudolf
| last2=Niederreiter | first2=Harald | authorlink2=Harald Niederreiter
| title=Finite Fields
| publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]
| date=1997
| edition=2nd
| isbn=978-0-521-39231-0}}</ref> has 141 articles authored or coauthored by Carlitz in its reference list.
